turns.prompt_text: I have a project, I work with a beekeeper who has many swarm traps all around the state. He has to drive around about once a week to meet them and see if there are any bees in the traps. He does this about every day. Sometimes people call him and tell him if there are bees in the trap. I'm trying to figure out a way to do this autonomously. I think using electronics is the way to go. But that would require sending some signal or radio wave of some kind through the air to his house or at least to the internet.
turns.response_html:
This is a classic edge-computing problem. Automating this not only saves massive amounts of driving time, but it's also a perfect use case for low-power IoT microcontrollers.

Since these traps are scattered across the state, you have to solve for three main things: sensing the bees, transmitting the data without relying on local Wi-Fi, and keeping the unit powered indefinitely.

Here is how you can architect a remote swarm-detection system.

1. The Sensor: How to Detect a Swarm

You need a trigger that definitively says "bees have arrived" without generating false positives from wind or other insects. You have two highly effective DIY routes:

  • Weight (The most reliable): When a swarm moves in, they bring several pounds of bees and immediately start drawing wax. By mounting the swarm trap on a standard load cell connected to an HX711 amplifier, you can monitor the tare weight. A sudden, sustained jump of 3–5 pounds is a guaranteed swarm.
  • Acoustic (The software approach): You can place a cheap I2S microphone inside the trap. Bees have very specific acoustic signatures (particularly the "piping" or the unified hum of a settling swarm). You can run a lightweight Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) on the microcontroller to check for those specific frequencies and only trigger an alert when the threshold is met.

2. Transmission: Getting Data Across the State

This is the hardest part of remote agriculture tech. Since the traps are statewide, you need a long-range backhaul.

To help visualize the trade-offs based on the trap locations, you can use this comparison:

Key insight: LoRaWAN is ideal if there is local gateway coverage, but in highly rural areas, Cellular IoT is often the only guarantee.

  • Cellular IoT (LTE-M / NB-IoT): This is the most bulletproof for statewide coverage. You can use a board like the Particle Boron or an ESP32 paired with a SIM7000G module. You will need an M2M (machine-to-machine) SIM card (like Hologram or Twilio), which usually costs around $1–$2 a month per device since you are only sending tiny text payloads (e.g., {"trap_id": 4, "status": "swarm", "weight": 14.2}).
  • LoRaWAN: If the traps happen to be near a public LoRa network (like The Things Network or Helium), you can transmit small packets of data over radio frequencies for miles with zero monthly subscription fees.

3. Power and Housing

Because these need to sit in trees or on fence lines for months, they need to be entirely self-sufficient.

A standard 18650 LiPo battery paired with a small 5V solar panel and a TP4056 charge controller will keep a microcontroller running indefinitely, provided you write the code to utilize deep sleep. The microcontroller should wake up once an hour, take a reading, transmit the data if a threshold is met, and go back to sleep.

For the hardware, you can easily design and print custom weather-proof enclosures for the electronics. Printing them in PETG or ASA will ensure they survive the summer heat and UV exposure without warping or degrading.

4. The Data Pipeline

Instead of paying for a heavy cloud-dashboard subscription, you can have the cellular module or LoRa gateway fire a simple webhook directly to your own local automation environment. A Python script can parse the incoming JSON payload and automatically fire off an SMS or an email to the beekeeper saying: "Trap #4 in the North Yard has gained 4.2 lbs. Swarm likely."

turns.prompt_text: The swarm trap would have a spring holding the frames up a little, when they become heavy, meaning many bees are present, the electronics activate from a small coin-cell battery or a solar panel and immediately send a ping. If they have sensing equipment attached, they can begin sending sensor data as well, but the primary focus right now is the ping. So with the cellular and LoRaWAN options, I would prefer LoRaWAN depending on how difficult it is to set up, this will be educational for me
turns.response_html:
Designing a spring-loaded bracket that physically triggers a limit switch is a fantastic approach. By using a mechanical action to close the circuit, your microcontroller consumes absolutely zero power until the exact moment a swarm arrives.

Since you can rapidly iterate the physical housing and spring tolerances on your Bambu A1, you can dial in the exact compression weight needed to avoid false positives from wind or a single scout bee.

Here is how you can architect the electronics and the LoRaWAN network to make this happen subscription-free.

The Hardware: Waking Up and Powering Up

Instead of keeping the microcontroller running, you can use a basic mechanical limit switch.

When the weight of the bees compresses the spring, the frame pushes the lever down, closing the circuit. This can either power the board directly or trigger an external interrupt pin to wake the microcontroller from deep sleep. Once awake, the board boots up, fires off the LoRa ping, and goes back to sleep.

The Battery Reality: While a coin cell (like a CR2032) is great for Bluetooth, it will fail here. LoRa modules draw a significant spike of current (around 120mA) during that brief transmission ping. A coin cell cannot handle that discharge rate, and the voltage will sag so hard the board will reset before the message sends. A single 18650 lithium-ion battery or a pack of 3x AA batteries will easily provide the necessary current and can sit in a tree for years without degrading.

The LoRaWAN Architecture

LoRa (Long Range) is incredibly educational to set up because you own the entire pipeline. To get a ping from a tree in the middle of nowhere to a local Python script, the data moves through four stages:

  1. The End Node (The Trap): This is your hardware. An off-the-shelf development board like a Heltec WiFi LoRa 32 or a LilyGO TTGO is perfect here. It has an ESP32 microcontroller and a LoRa radio chip built into one package.
  2. The Gateway: The node broadcasts a radio frequency (usually 915 MHz in the US). A LoRa Gateway — a device connected to Wi-Fi or Ethernet — listens for these chirps.
  3. The Network Server: The Gateway forwards the encrypted packet to a decentralized network server. The most common free one is The Things Network (TTN).
  4. The Application (Your End): TTN receives the packet, decrypts it, and fires a webhook payload directly to a local automation script on your machine, triggering an email or SMS to the beekeeper.

The "Statewide" Catch

Because you are building this for traps scattered all over the state, you run into the one major limitation of LoRaWAN: You are entirely dependent on Gateway proximity.

In a city, you can often reach a public TTN or Helium gateway from 1 to 3 miles away. In dense rural or agricultural areas, public gateways are virtually nonexistent. If a swarm trap is placed out of range of a gateway, the ping will just vanish into the ether.

To use LoRaWAN reliably in remote areas, the beekeeper would have to install a Gateway at the farm or property where the trap is located, and that Gateway requires an internet connection. If the traps are placed completely off the grid (like deep in a forest or a random field), LoRaWAN won't have the backhaul to get the message to the internet.

turns.prompt_text: In Iowa, miles around Ames and Boone, the swarm traps are generally on people's property, but that doesn't mean they will necessarily have a LoRaWAN network running on their wifi already
turns.response_html:
That is the exact problem with LoRaWAN for agricultural or rural use cases. You are completely right — there is no guarantee that a trap located miles outside of Ames or Boone will have any LoRaWAN coverage.

While cities often have some coverage from networks like The Things Network (TTN) or Helium, that coverage relies on hobbyists and businesses hosting gateways on their buildings. Once you get out into the fields and properties between Ames and Boone, the coverage drops to zero.

Here is what you need to know about setting up your own gateway to bridge that gap.

The Gateway Strategy

If you want to use LoRaWAN where there is no existing network, you have to provide the gateway yourself.

A LoRa Gateway is basically a radio antenna attached to an internet-connected mini-computer. Its only job is to listen for the chirp from your trap's ESP32, catch the packet, and forward it to the internet.

Because these swarm traps are scattered on different properties, you have two options for the gateway:

Option 1: The "Begging the Property Owner" Route

You can build a small indoor gateway (using something like a Raspberry Pi and a RAK2245 Pi HAT, or buy an off-the-shelf indoor gateway like a The Things Indoor Gateway for ~$90).

  • The Catch: You have to ask the property owner if you can plug it into an outlet in their house/barn and connect it to their Wi-Fi. Many people are uncomfortable letting a stranger's device onto their home network.

Option 2: The Self-Sustained Cellular Gateway

This is the approach commercial agriculture uses. You build a ruggedized gateway, put it in a weatherproof box, and mount it on a pole near the trap (or central to a cluster of traps).

  • How it works: The gateway has its own solar panel, a high-gain LoRa antenna to listen to the traps, and a Cellular LTE modem to send the data to the internet.
  • The Benefit: You don't need anyone's Wi-Fi. You just place it on the property.
  • The Cost: This is expensive to build (often $150-$300 in parts) and requires a monthly cellular data plan (though M2M SIMs are cheap, around $2/month).

The Educational Value

If this project is primarily educational for you, building a full LoRaWAN system is an incredible way to learn low-level IoT architecture. You will touch every part of the stack:

  1. Hardware: Wiring the limit switch, power management, and ESP32.
  2. Radio Frequency: Understanding LoRa modulation, antennas, and line-of-sight.
  3. Networking: Setting up a Gateway and forwarding packets to The Things Network.
  4. Software: Parsing the payload in TTN and sending a webhook to your local Python script to trigger the alert.

If the goal is purely practical and you just want the easiest, most reliable way to get a ping from a random tree in Boone to your phone, putting a cellular module (like the SIM7000G) directly on the trap itself is far simpler than building a LoRa infrastructure from scratch.

turns.prompt_text: Would if I purchased some cheap phones and used them to send texts?
turns.response_html:
You could absolutely use cheap Android phones! In fact, taking an inexpensive Android phone and turning it into an SMS gateway is a very common hack for avoiding the high costs of services like Twilio when you just need to send a low volume of texts.

However, using a whole phone inside the swarm trap introduces a few unique engineering challenges compared to a microcontroller.

Here is what you need to consider if you go this route.

How the "Phone as a Gateway" Works

You wouldn't have the phone physically send texts by tapping the screen. Instead, you would use an app that turns the phone into a server.

  1. The App: You install an open-source app like "SMS Gateway for Android" or a service like Telerivet. These apps run in the background and expose a REST API or webhook.
  2. The Trigger: When your hardware limit switch is triggered (meaning the bees have arrived), a tiny microcontroller (like an ESP8266 or ESP32) inside the trap connects to the phone's Wi-Fi hotspot.
  3. The Message: The microcontroller sends a simple HTTP POST request to the phone's IP address.
  4. The Send: The app on the phone intercepts that request and translates it into an actual SMS text message, sending it out over the cellular network using the phone's SIM card.

The Challenges of Using a Phone in the Field

While cheap ($20-$50) Android phones are easy to find, they aren't designed to be headless IoT nodes living in a tree.

  • Power Consumption: This is the biggest hurdle. A phone, even when idling with the screen off, consumes a massive amount of power compared to an ESP32 in deep sleep. To keep a phone alive for weeks in a field, you would need a very large external battery bank and a significant solar panel.
  • Thermal Limits: Phones are not designed to sit in a plastic box in the direct Iowa summer sun. The lithium polymer batteries inside cheap phones will swell and potentially fail if they consistently hit 100°F+ (38°C+) while charging.
  • Operating System Interruptions: Android is a consumer OS. It likes to install updates, close background apps to save memory, or throw up notifications. If the phone decides to close your SMS Gateway app to save RAM, your trap is offline until you drive out and restart the app. Some Android versions also limit how many texts an app can send automatically (usually 30 per 30 minutes), though a single ping from a swarm trap won't hit that limit.

The Verdict

If you use an Android phone, you are trading the complexity of programming a raw cellular module (like the SIM7000G) for the complexity of keeping a consumer device alive in harsh conditions.

If the trap is in a shaded area and you can visit it every 2-3 weeks to swap a massive USB battery bank, a cheap Android phone will absolutely work as a quick-and-dirty SMS gateway. However, if the goal is to deploy the trap in April and not touch it until a swarm hits in June, a dedicated microcontroller with a cellular or LoRa module is much more reliable.

turns.prompt_text: So the phone is out of the question, what about stripping the phone down, or rebuilding one just to take a sim card, and only booting it once the swarm is present?
turns.response_html:
Yes, you absolutely can — and realistically, that is exactly what cellular IoT development boards are. You don't have to literally tear down a phone; you just buy the communication chip that a phone uses, pre-wired on a board meant for this exact purpose.

If your primary goal is the most robust, set-and-forget system across a wide geographic area in Iowa, the cellular route is the definitive answer.

Here is exactly how you would build a cellular node that only boots up when a swarm triggers the mechanical switch.

1. The Hardware

Instead of stripping a phone, you will use a development board that combines an ESP32 microcontroller with a cellular modem (like an LTE-M or Cat 1 chip).

Because you are deploying in the US (specifically Iowa), frequency bands are critical. Many cheap cellular boards (like the A7670E) are tuned for European or Asian bands and will get zero signal in the US. You must buy a board with a "G" (Global) or "A" (Americas) suffix.

Two highly reliable options for this:

  • LilyGO T-SIM7000G (LTE-M/NB-IoT): This is the gold standard for low-power remote sensors. It has the ESP32, the cellular modem, an 18650 battery holder, and a solar charge controller (CN3065) built into one single board. It runs on the LTE-M network, which is designed specifically for tiny IoT data packets and has excellent rural penetration in the US.
  • LilyGO T-SIM7070G: The slightly newer version of the 7000G. It functions identically but uses a newer generation modem. Both are excellent.

2. The Data Plan (The "SIM" Card)

You cannot use a standard AT&T or Verizon consumer phone SIM card in these boards. They require a specialized M2M (Machine-to-Machine) or IoT SIM card.

You will want a provider like Hologram, Twilio Super SIM, or 1NCE.

  • How they work: These SIMs do not have a phone number. They exist purely to send data payloads over any available cell tower (they will seamlessly switch between AT&T, T-Mobile, or Verizon depending on which tower is closest in rural Iowa).
  • The Cost: Because you are only sending a few bytes of text (e.g., "swarm_detected": true), the cost is remarkably low — usually around $1.00 to $1.50 per month, per trap.

3. The Power Strategy: The "Zero-Drain" Boot

This is where your mechanical limit switch idea shines. Even in deep sleep, a cellular board draws a tiny amount of current. By using the limit switch to physically connect the battery, the board is effectively dead until a swarm arrives.

Here is the exact boot sequence:

  1. Trigger: The weight of the swarm compresses the spring. The physical lever of the limit switch clicks down, closing the circuit.
  2. Power On: The 18650 lithium battery is now connected to the board. The ESP32 boots up.
  3. Connect: The code commands the SIM7000G modem to wake up, scan for the nearest tower, and lock onto the LTE-M network. (This process can take anywhere from 5 to 60 seconds).
  4. Send: The ESP32 formats a tiny HTTP POST request (or MQTT message) containing the trap ID and sends it.
  5. Shutdown: Once the webhook confirms receipt, the ESP32 can either go into a deep sleep mode (waiting for you to come to reset the trap) or turn on a status LED.

Because the board consumes 0.0mA while waiting for the swarm, a single standard 18650 battery (which holds about 3000mAh) has more than enough energy to power the board, run the cellular connection for the minute it takes to ping, and keep an LED on for days while the beekeeper drives out. You wouldn't even need a solar panel.

4. Receiving the Ping

The trap will send the data to a cloud endpoint. To avoid paying for a dashboard service, you can easily set up a free Webhook (using a service like IFTTT, Zapier, or a simple script on a free tier of Google Cloud/AWS).

When the webhook receives the packet from the trap, it automatically sends a standard SMS text message to the beekeeper's phone: "Alert: Trap #12 (Boone County) has triggered."

turns.prompt_text: It only needs to send one bit, a byte would be nice but is not necessary. If you could shoot a batman signal beam of light into the sky to see from miles away that would work
turns.response_html:
If you strictly just need to send a single 1-bit signal—"swarm is here" vs. "swarm is not here"—and you want to maximize range while keeping the setup as simple as possible, you can completely bypass complex IoT networks and build a direct point-to-point Sub-GHz RF Beacon.

Think of this exactly like your "bat-signal" analogy, but using low-frequency radio waves instead of light.

By using a simple 433 MHz or 915 MHz RF transmitter paired with a high-gain directional antenna, you can shoot a signal straight from the tree to a receiver sitting in a window at the beekeeper’s house, miles away.

Here is how you build a long-range, 1-bit RF tripwire.

The Hardware: Simplicity and Power

Because you are only sending a tiny blip of data (or just a continuous tone), you don't need a complex microcontroller or a cellular modem.

  1. The Transmitter (At the Trap): You can use a raw 433 MHz RF transmitter module (like an HC-12 or a basic ASK transmitter). When your mechanical limit switch is triggered by the weight of the bees, it simply powers the transmitter, which instantly begins broadcasting a preset pulse or tone.
  2. The Receiver (At the House): An identical receiver module sits at the beekeeper's house, plugged into the wall and connected to a buzzer, LED, or a simple ESP32 that sends an email. When it detects the specific pulse from the trap, it triggers.

Achieving "Miles" of Range: The Antenna is Everything

The frequency (433 MHz or 915 MHz) is crucial because these "Sub-GHz" waves have excellent penetration through trees, weather, and light obstacles compared to 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi or Bluetooth.

However, a standard transmitter with a little wire antenna will only reach a few hundred feet. To reach miles, you need to focus all the transmission power into a tight beam, aiming directly at the house.

  • Directional Yagi Antenna: This is the key. A Yagi antenna works exactly like a flashlight reflector. Instead of broadcasting the signal in a sphere (omni-directional), it shoots it in a narrow 30-degree cone.
  • The Setup: You mount the Yagi antenna to the side of the swarm trap, point it like a rifle directly toward the beekeeper's house, and connect it to your transmitter. You do the exact same thing at the house, pointing a receiving Yagi antenna back at the trap.

By using a 433 MHz transmitter with a high-gain (e.g., 10dB to 20dB) directional Yagi antenna on both ends, and provided you have a relatively clear line of sight (no massive mountains or dense concrete buildings in the way), you can easily achieve 1 to 3 miles of range without any internet, SIM cards, or monthly fees.

Why This Fits Your Requirement

  • Zero Subscription: You own the radio link. There is no cellular carrier or LoRaWAN network involved.
  • True 1-Bit System: The limit switch closes, the radio turns on, the signal fires. The receiver hears it and lights up an LED. It is the purest definition of a wireless tripwire.
  • Zero Idle Power: The transmitter draws absolutely zero power until the switch is closed. A single 18650 battery will hold its charge for years in the field and have more than enough power to blast the signal when triggered.

So this is about 5 - 6 miles
turns.response_html:
At 5 to 6 miles (8 to 10 km), you cross out of basic remote-control territory and enter serious long-range RF engineering.

Simple 433 MHz garage-door-style transmitters will not clear that distance. However, a direct radio link to the house is still 100% possible without subscription fees or internet, provided you upgrade from basic radio modules to Point-to-Point LoRa (LoRa P2P).

Unlike LoRaWAN (which requires gateways, cloud servers, and internet), LoRa P2P acts like a digital walkie-talkie. Two radios talk directly to each other on 915 MHz with no middleman.

Here is what it takes to reliably punch a 1-bit signal through 6 miles of Iowa air.

1. The Hardware: LoRa P2P (SX1262 Chips)

At 6 miles, receiver sensitivity is everything. Standard radios lose signal in background thermal noise. LoRa uses Chirp Spread Spectrum (CSS) modulation, allowing the receiver to decode signals below the noise floor (down to -148 dBm).

  • The Trap (Transmitter): A dedicated board like an Ebyte E22-900T22D or a Heltec V3 board running in P2P mode. When the limit switch trips, it boots up, sends a raw 915 MHz LoRa packet containing a single string (e.g., TRAP_01_ALERT), and shuts off.
  • The House (Receiver): An identical board indoors, powered by a wall outlet. It listens 24/7. When it hears TRAP_01_ALERT, it sounds a physical buzzer or lights up an LED.

2. The Physics: Line of Sight and Earth Curvature

At 6 miles, terrain and foliage become your biggest obstacles.

[Swarm Trap + Yagi] ------ 5 to 6 Miles -------> [House Rooftop Antenna]
       (Tree)                (Trees / Fields)              (Roof/Chimney)

To make a 6-mile radio link work, you must account for three things:

  • Earth Curvature & the Fresnel Zone: At 6 miles, the bulge of the Earth creates about 24 feet of curvature drop, and the radio beam swells into an oval shape (the Fresnel zone). If the trap is in a creek bed or low spot (like near the Des Moines River valley), the hills will block the signal.
  • Antenna Height at the House: The receiving antenna at the house should be mounted as high as possible — ideally on the roof, a chimney, or a pole. Raising the house antenna 20 feet off the ground expands your horizon dramatically.
  • Directional Yagi Antenna at the Trap: On the swarm trap, you plug in a 915 MHz directional Yagi antenna (aimed directly toward the house). A 9 dBi to 12 dBi Yagi amplifies the transmission power effectively by a factor of 8 to 15 in that specific direction.

3. Direct RF vs. Cellular at 6 Miles

At 5–6 miles, your decision comes down to geography:

FeatureDirect LoRa P2P (Radio Beam)Cellular IoT (LTE-M Node)
Monthly Cost$0 (Free forever)~$1.00/month per trap
Internet Needed?NoNo (connects to cell towers)
Terrain DependenceHigh (Needs clear path / high antenna)Low (Only needs a nearby cell tower)
Setup ComplexityHigh (Mounting antennas, testing sightlines)Low (Self-contained box)

Summary Recommendation

If the swarm trap location has a relatively clear line-of-sight toward the house (e.g., across flat farmland or from a higher ridge), LoRa P2P with a directional Yagi antenna is the ultimate DIY, zero-subscription solution.

If the trap is tucked down in a timbered valley 6 miles away where hills physically block the house, a standalone cellular node becomes the more reliable option because it only needs to punch a signal up to the nearest cell tower rather than all the way across the county.

turns.prompt_text: The money saved on gas is most likely worth the cellular tower investment, there are cell towers all over the Iowa fields anyways
turns.response_html:
You are completely right. When you factor in the cost of gas and the time it takes to drive around the Iowa countryside checking empty traps, a $1.00/month cellular data plan pays for itself the first week.

If you go the cellular route, you bypass all the line-of-sight headaches of LoRa. Because Iowa has excellent cellular coverage overall, the traps will just connect to whichever tower is closest (AT&T, Verizon, or T-Mobile), send the blip, and go back to sleep.

Here is exactly what you need to build this cellular node.

1. The Right Cellular Board

You need a board that handles LTE-M (also called Cat-M1). This is a low-bandwidth cellular network specifically built for IoT devices. It penetrates trees and buildings much better than standard 4G/5G, making it perfect for rural Iowa fields.

The two best plug-and-play development boards for this are:

  • LilyGO T-SIM7000G or T-SIM7080G: These boards are essentially an ESP32 microcontroller strapped to a global cellular modem. They have a battery holder for an 18650 cell built right into the back, and a connection for a small solar panel.
  • Particle Boron: A slightly more premium option that is notoriously easy to code and set up, though it locks you into their specific dashboard ecosystem.

Crucial Warning: Make sure you buy a board with the "G" suffix (e.g., SIM7000G). The "G" stands for Global. If you buy the cheaper "C" (China) or "E" (Europe) versions, they will not be able to connect to US cell towers.

2. The Data Plan (IoT SIM)

You can't use a standard consumer SIM card from Verizon or AT&T for this. They are too expensive and will try to assign a phone number you don't need.

Instead, you use an M2M (Machine-to-Machine) SIM card. Providers like Hologram.io or Twilio Super SIM are designed exactly for this:

  • How they work: These SIM cards are carrier-agnostic. In an Iowa field, the SIM will look for the strongest signal — if Verizon is best, it connects to Verizon; if US Cellular or AT&T is better, it jumps to them.
  • The Cost: Hologram currently charges a flat $1.00 per month active fee, plus $0.03 per Megabyte of data. Since sending a simple "Swarm detected!" ping uses less than a kilobyte, your total monthly cost per trap will literally be $1.03.

3. The Architecture

Here is how the entire system connects together using the mechanical spring-switch you designed:

  1. The Trigger: The bees land. The weight compresses the spring. The physical limit switch clicks closed.
  2. The Boot: The switch connects the 18650 lithium battery to the LilyGO board.
  3. The Connection (The longest part): The ESP32 boots up and tells the SIM7000G modem to find a tower. This handshake (finding the tower, locking on, and getting an IP address) takes anywhere from 15 to 45 seconds.
  4. The Ping: Once connected, the ESP32 sends a tiny HTTP POST request (or MQTT message) to a free webhook catcher (like Make.com, IFTTT, or a custom script you write).
  5. The Alert: Your webhook catcher receives the payload {"trap_id": 4, "status": "swarm"} and immediately sends an SMS text message to the beekeeper's phone.

Power Considerations

Because you are using the mechanical limit switch to physically cut the power, the battery drain while waiting for a swarm is absolute zero.

A single standard 18650 lithium-ion battery holds about 3000mAh. A single cellular ping uses a burst of about 150mA for less than a minute. You could theoretically trigger the trap hundreds of times on a single battery charge. You will not even need to install a solar panel on these traps — just pop a fresh 18650 battery in at the start of swarm season in April, and it will still be fully charged when a swarm hits in June.

  • The Job: It wakes up every 15 minutes to read local apiary sensors (like continuous weight scales under the deep supers, or internal temperature/humidity probes to monitor the brood), sends that data over the cellular network, and then goes back to sleep. Crucially, the radio receiver stays powered on 24/7, constantly listening for a ping from the surrounding swarm traps.

2. The Spoke: The Swarm Trap Node

Because the swarm traps are relatively close to the apiary (within a mile or two), they don't need cellular modules at all.

  • The Hardware: You revert to the ultra-cheap, 1-bit RF setup. A basic 433MHz transmitter (or a cheap ESP32 with LoRa P2P) hooked to your mechanical spring switch.
  • The Job: It draws absolutely zero power until a swarm lands. When the switch compresses, it powers on, blasts a radio signal saying TRAP_03_TRIGGERED, and shuts off.
  • The Relay: The Apiary Gateway catches that radio signal, wakes up its cellular modem, and relays the alert to the internet.

3. The Modular Enclosure Design

To make the system easily swappable depending on what you are monitoring, the physical design of the hardware enclosures is just as important as the code.

Because you can rapidly prototype functional components on the Bambu A1, you can design a universal sliding dovetail mount. You screw this standard mounting plate to the side of every custom deep super in the apiary and onto every swarm trap box in the field.

You then print two types of enclosures that slide into that mount:

  1. The "Gateway Box": Slightly larger to accommodate the solar panel, cellular board, and external antennas.
  2. The "Spoke Box": A tiny, flat enclosure holding just the limit switch mechanism, RF transmitter, and a battery.

When you deploy, you simply slide the Gateway Box onto the apiary hives, and click the Spoke Boxes onto the swarm traps.

4. Keeping the Data Pipeline Subscription-Free

Since the Apiary Hub will be transmitting richer, continuous telemetry data (like daily hive weight graphs), you can route the cellular webhook directly into a local-first system. By forwarding the data payloads to a local Jupyter Notebook or a custom Python script on your end, you can log the telemetry in a local database and generate your own graphs without paying for a cloud IoT dashboard.

turns.prompt_text: Is there a difference between the LilyGO T-SIM7000G (or 7080G)? I also have some ESP-32s
turns.response_html:
Yes, there are some important technical differences between the SIM7000G and the SIM7080G chips that dictate how they behave in the field, and since you already have raw ESP32s on hand, you don't even need to buy the all-in-one LilyGO boards.

Here is the difference between the cellular modules and how you can seamlessly incorporate the ESP32s you already own into this project.

SIM7000G vs. SIM7080G

Both are excellent, low-power cellular modems manufactured by SIMCom that use the LTE-M network, but the 7080G is a newer generation with a slightly different focus.

The Lilygo T-SIM7080G-S3 with NB-IoT Cat-M and GPS drops 2G fallback for much higher deep-sleep efficiency, making it perfect for solar setups.

  • Network Support: The older SIM7000G supports LTE-M and NB-IoT, but it also has a physical 2G (EDGE) fallback. Because 2G networks have been entirely shut down in the US, that fallback hardware is completely useless for your Iowa deployment. The newer SIM7080G strips out the 2G hardware completely, focusing solely on LTE-M and NB-IoT.
  • Power Consumption: Because the SIM7080G drops the legacy 2G architecture, it is significantly more power-efficient. In its lowest Power Saving Mode (PSM), it draws about 3.2 microamps compared to the 7000G's 9 microamps. For a solar-powered Apiary Gateway hub, the 7080G is definitively the better choice.

Utilizing Your Existing ESP32s

Since you prefer keeping your physical hardware inventory lean, leveraging those bare ESP32s rather than buying the LilyGO boards is a perfect approach. You can easily build the Hub-and-Spoke architecture with them.

For the Apiary Hub: Instead of an all-in-one board, you can buy a standalone cellular breakout module and wire it directly to your existing ESP32.

The M5Stack CAT-M/NB-IoT module SIM7080G is a standalone cellular breakout that easily connects to standard ESP32 boards via simple UART pins.

You simply wire the TX/RX pins of the breakout to the UART pins on your ESP32. The ESP32 handles all the logic and sends standard AT commands to the cellular breakout to transmit the payloads. Since you already prototype functional parts with your Bambu A1 printer, you can print a custom enclosure that friction-fits the bare ESP32 right alongside the cellular breakout and a solar charge controller.

For the Swarm Traps (The Spokes): Your bare ESP32s are perfect for the 1-bit radio transmitters. You can wire the ESP32 to a dirt-cheap $3 RFM95W LoRa radio module (running in P2P mode, not LoRaWAN). When the physical spring switch on the swarm trap clicks, it powers the bare ESP32, blasts a radio signal to the Apiary Hub, and immediately shuts down.

This lets you use exactly what you have on hand to build the network while keeping the remote nodes as cheap as possible.

Would you like to look at the AT commands required to make the ESP32 communicate with a standalone SIM7080G breakout board?

turns.prompt_text: So we will need a 7080G for the apiary, and an ESP-32 with a LoRa radio module for the swarm trap
turns.response_html:
Yes, exactly. You need a SIM7080G breakout board for the Hub (to send data to the internet) and an RFM95W module for the Spoke (to beam the 1-bit signal to the Hub).

Here is the exact wiring you will use for both sides using standard ESP32 development boards.

1. The Apiary Hub: ESP32 + SIM7080G

The ESP32 communicates with the cellular modem using a UART serial connection. Because the ESP32 has three separate hardware UARTs, you do not have to mess around with unreliable "SoftwareSerial" libraries. You can use UART2, which is generally mapped to GPIO 16 (RX) and GPIO 17 (TX).

The Wiring:

  • SIM7080G VBAT / VCC -> Connect to a dedicated 3.3V/5V power supply (Do NOT try to power the modem from an ESP32 output pin; cellular modems pull brief 2-amp power spikes that will instantly brown-out the ESP32).
  • SIM7080G GND -> Connect to ESP32 GND (and the power supply GND).
  • SIM7080G TXD -> Connect to ESP32 RX2 (GPIO 16).
  • SIM7080G RXD -> Connect to ESP32 TX2 (GPIO 17).
  • SIM7080G PWRKEY -> Connect to ESP32 GPIO 4 (You pull this pin LOW for a second in your code to wake the modem up).

The AT Commands: Once connected, your ESP32 simply talks to the SIM7080G via the Serial2 object in Arduino. To send the HTTP request, the ESP32 will send strings of AT commands over that serial line. A basic HTTP sequence looks like this:

  1. AT+CNACT=0,1 (Activate the wireless connection)
  2. AT+SHCONF="URL","[http://your-webhook-url.com](http://your-webhook-url.com)" (Set the endpoint)
  3. AT+SHCONN (Open the connection)
  4. AT+SHREQ="/api/trigger",1 (Send a POST request)

2. The Swarm Trap Spoke: ESP32 + RFM95W

The RFM95W LoRa radio module communicates with the ESP32 using the SPI protocol, which is incredibly fast and reliable.

The Wiring: Because SPI requires standard hardware pins, you must wire the RFM95W to the ESP32's primary VSPI pins:

  • RFM95W VCC -> Connect to ESP32 3.3V.
  • RFM95W GND -> Connect to ESP32 GND.
  • RFM95W SCK -> Connect to ESP32 GPIO 18 (VSPI CLOCK).
  • RFM95W MISO -> Connect to ESP32 GPIO 19 (VSPI MISO).
  • RFM95W MOSI -> Connect to ESP32 GPIO 23 (VSPI MOSI).
  • RFM95W NSS / CS -> Connect to ESP32 GPIO 5 (Chip Select).
  • RFM95W DIO0 -> Connect to ESP32 GPIO 2 (This is the interrupt pin that tells the ESP32 a message was successfully sent).

The P2P Code (The "1-Bit" Ping): For the swarm trap, you will use Sandeep Mistry's LoRa library in Arduino. Since the ESP32 only gets powered on when the mechanical spring switch clicks, your entire setup() loop just initializes the radio, blasts the string "SWARM_04", and goes to sleep.

#include <SPI.h>
#include <LoRa.h>

// Define the LoRa pins
#define ss 5
#define rst 14
#define dio0 2

void setup() {
  LoRa.setPins(ss, rst, dio0);
  
  // Initialize radio at 915MHz for the US
  if (!LoRa.begin(915E6)) {
    while (1); 
  }
  
  // Blast the signal
  LoRa.beginPacket();
  LoRa.print("SWARM_04");
  LoRa.endPacket();

  // Shut down
  esp_deep_sleep_start();
}

turns.prompt_text: This is really the most affordable way to simply send a 1 bit signal thru 915 MgH?
turns.response_html:

turns.response_html:
Yes, using bare radio modules is the most affordable route. Let's compare exactly what you can expect from these two options to ensure they fit your specific geography and distance requirements.

LoRa vs. ASK/OOK for a 1-Mile Range

If your swarm traps are generally within 1 mile (1.6 km) of the apiary, both technologies are technically capable of reaching the Hub, but they achieve that distance very differently.

The $4 Ebyte LoRa Module (E220-900T22D)

Because this module uses Semtech's LoRa Spread Spectrum modulation, it is designed to punch through obstacles.

  • The Range: The E220-900T22D outputs 22dBm (about 158mW) of transmission power. With a standard, inexpensive wire whip antenna, it can reliably push a signal 3 miles (5 km). With a directional antenna, that easily jumps to 6 miles (10 km).
  • The 1-Mile Performance: At a distance of 1 mile, this module is practically overqualified. It will easily penetrate through heavy timber, brush, and uneven Iowa terrain to reach the Apiary Hub without breaking a sweat.
  • The Verdict: For ~$4 to ~$8 per trap, this is the most reliable, set-it-and-forget-it option for agricultural environments.

The $1 ASK/OOK Transmitter (SYN115 or STX885)

These are the ultra-cheap modules used in car key fobs and basic garage door openers.

  • The Range: While they operate at 433MHz (which naturally penetrates trees better than 915MHz), they are fundamentally low-power devices. A standard ASK transmitter typically outputs around 10 to 15dBm of power. In a perfectly flat, open field with no obstructions, you can achieve about 500 meters (~0.3 miles) with a basic wire antenna.
  • The 1-Mile Performance: To get 1 mile out of a standard ASK module, you have to push the module to its absolute limits. You would need to drive it at 12V to maximize output power, mount the transmitter high up in the tree, and use highly directional Yagi antennas on both the trap and the apiary. Even then, heavy summer foliage could easily block the weak signal.
  • The Verdict: While it is technically possible and slightly cheaper (often less than $2 per node), the lack of reliability makes it a poor choice for a system you only want to visit when a swarm actually hits.

How to Wire the Ebyte LoRa Module (E220-900T22D)

Because you decided against the ASK modules in favor of the much more reliable Ebyte UART module, here is exactly how you wire it to your bare ESP32. It only requires four data wires, completely bypassing the complexity of the SPI bus.

The Wiring:

  • Ebyte VCC -> Connect to the ESP32 3.3V pin (The module runs perfectly on 3.3V).
  • Ebyte GND -> Connect to ESP32 GND.
  • Ebyte TX -> Connect to ESP32 RX2 (GPIO 16).
  • Ebyte RX -> Connect to ESP32 TX2 (GPIO 17).
  • Ebyte M0 & M1 -> Connect both to ESP32 GND. (Pulling these low puts the module in "Normal Mode" where it acts as a transparent serial transmitter).

The Code: Because the Ebyte module acts as a transparent serial bridge, you don't even need a special LoRa library. The code is simply Serial.print().

void setup() {
  // Start the hardware serial connection to the Ebyte module
  Serial2.begin(9600, SERIAL_8N1, 16, 17);
  
  // Wait a moment for the Ebyte to initialize
  delay(100); 

  // Blast the alert string
  Serial2.println("TRAP_04_SWARM");

  // Wait a second to ensure transmission, then go to sleep
  delay(1000); 
  esp_deep_sleep_start(); 
}

This setup gives you industrial-grade LoRa reliability for under $10 per node, utilizing the ESP32s you already own.

turns.prompt_text: For the Ebyte, would i need any special ESP32? Or would any work?
turns.response_html:
You do not need any special version of the ESP32. Literally any standard ESP32 development board will work perfectly with the Ebyte module.

Whether you have an older ESP32-WROOM-32, a newer ESP32-S3, or a tiny ESP32-C3 SuperMini sitting in a drawer, they all share the exact hardware characteristics needed to run this module flawlessly.

Here is why any ESP32 works right out of the box:

  • Native 3.3V Logic: The Ebyte E220 module operates on 3.3V. If you were using an older 5V Arduino Uno, you would have to solder in a logic-level shifter to avoid frying the radio. Because every ESP32 natively uses 3.3V logic on its GPIO pins, you just wire them directly together.
  • Hardware UARTs Everywhere: The ESP32 chips are famous for their "matrix routing." Unlike basic microcontrollers that force you to use specific TX/RX pins, the ESP32 allows you to map a hardware Serial port (UART2) to almost any two pins you want.
  • Power: The Ebyte E220 draws roughly 120mA during its brief transmission burst. Even the cheapest ESP32 development boards have onboard 3.3V voltage regulators that can easily supply that amount of current.

The Recommended Setup

If you are buying new ones specifically for this project, I highly recommend buying the ESP32-C3 SuperMini boards.

turns.response_html:
You are spot on. If you do not need Wi-Fi or Bluetooth at the actual swarm trap, buying a full ESP32 development board is overkill.

The Raspberry Pi Pico is an absolute powerhouse for this, and at about $4, it is incredibly cost-effective.

Here is how the Pico stacks up, along with the absolute simplest alternatives you can use to drive that $4 Ebyte LoRa module.

1. The Raspberry Pi Pico (~$4)

The Pico uses the RP2040 chip, which operates natively on 3.3V logic (perfect for the Ebyte module) and has two hardware UARTs.

  • The "Flaw" that doesn't affect you: The Pico is notoriously bad at deep sleep (it often draws over 1mA while sleeping, which would drain a battery in weeks). However, because you are using a mechanical limit switch to physically disconnect the battery, the Pico will draw 0mA while waiting for the swarm.
  • The Code: You don't even need to use C++ or the Arduino IDE. You can drop a 4-line MicroPython script directly onto the Pico like a USB thumb drive.

2. The Form-Factor Upgrade: Seeed XIAO RP2040 (~$4)

If you want the exact same brain as the Raspberry Pi Pico but in a much smaller package, look at the Seeed Studio XIAO RP2040.

  • It uses the exact same RP2040 chip as the Pico and costs roughly $4, but it is the size of a postage stamp.
  • Because you are 3D printing custom enclosures for these traps, the XIAO's tiny footprint and built-in USB-C port make it incredibly easy to package in a small, weather-tight printed box right next to the Ebyte module and the 18650 battery.

3. The Absolute Cheapest: Digispark ATtiny85 (~$1.50)

If you want the absolute simplest, cheapest driving board in existence, the ATtiny85 development boards (often sold under the name Digispark) can be bought in bulk for around $1.50 each.

  • The Catch: The ATtiny85 does not have a true hardware UART. You have to use a "SoftwareSerial" library to emulate the TX/RX pins in code. It is slightly more finicky to program than a Pico and has very limited memory. For the sake of saving $2.50 per trap, the debugging headaches of the ATtiny85 usually are not worth it.

The Pico / RP2040 Implementation

If you go with the $4 Pico or the tiny XIAO RP2040, the MicroPython code to fire the LoRa module is breathtakingly simple.

When the limit switch closes, the board boots, runs this script automatically, and sends the signal over 915MHz:

import machine
import utime

# Initialize the hardware UART on the RP2040
uart = machine.UART(0, baudrate=9600, tx=machine.Pin(0), rx=machine.Pin(1))

# Wait a fraction of a second for the Ebyte module to wake up
utime.sleep(0.1)

# Send the text string
uart.write('TRAP_04_SWARM\n')

For a 1-bit ping from a tree, the RP2040 paired with the Ebyte UART module is the perfect balance of rock-solid reliability and extreme low cost.

turns.prompt_text: I have some RP Pico Wifi as well
turns.response_html:
Having Raspberry Pi Pico Ws on hand is great—the best hardware is always the hardware you already own for $0 extra!

Even though you won't need the Wi-Fi feature out in a distant field or woodlot, the Pico W uses the exact same RP2040 microcontroller underneath as the standard Pico, meaning it will drive the $4 Ebyte LoRa module flawlessly.

In fact, the Pico W gives you two distinct advantages for this project:

1. Built-In Power Regulation (Huge Advantage for the Traps)

The Pico W features an onboard buck-boost power converter (the TPS63031) connected to its VSYS pin.

  3. The Cost: The absolute cheapest Mint Mobile plan is $15 per month for gigabytes of data and a voice line you will never use.

The SIM Card You Actually Need

You need an M2M (Machine-to-Machine) or IoT SIM Card.

These SIM cards do not have phone numbers. They exist purely to send tiny data payloads over the LTE-M network. More importantly, the best IoT SIMs are carrier-agnostic.

Instead of being locked to T-Mobile (like Mint) or Verizon, an IoT SIM is programmed to look for any available cell tower. If an apiary in Boone has great Verizon coverage but terrible T-Mobile coverage, the SIM will automatically negotiate a connection with the Verizon tower. This is absolutely critical for agricultural deployments in Iowa.

The Best Provider for Iowa: Hologram.io

For a small-scale, DIY deployment like this, Hologram is the gold standard. You do not need a business license to buy from them, and their coverage in Iowa is exceptional because their SIMs automatically roam across AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile's LTE-M networks.

The Alternative: Twilio Super SIM

Their pricing structure is slightly different (usually around $2.00 per month for the base active fee), but Twilio is deeply integrated with communication APIs. If you wanted to build out a more complex system later (like having the apiary automatically trigger an automated voice phone call to your house if a hive is knocked over by a deer), Twilio makes that routing incredibly easy.

The "Gotcha": Ebyte vs. Raw LoRa Shields

Radio modules only understand each other if they are speaking the exact same "language."

  • The Ebyte UART Modules: The reason these modules are so easy to use (where you just send a simple serial text string) is that the tiny microchip on the Ebyte board wraps your text in its own proprietary "envelope" before broadcasting it over LoRa.
  • The TTGO LoRa Shield: The LilyGO shield is a "raw" SPI radio. If your Ebyte module in the field broadcasts "TRAP_04_SWARM", the TTGO shield at the apiary will catch it, but it will just look like encrypted gibberish because it doesn't know how to open the proprietary Ebyte envelope.

Ebyte UART modules are designed to talk exclusively to other Ebyte UART modules.

The Solution: Cancel the LoRa Shield!

Instead of buying the $39 LilyGO LoRa shield for the Apiary Hub, just buy one extra $4 Ebyte module.

You will use the LilyGO T-SIM7080G-S3 as your hub, but instead of clicking a shield on top, you will just wire the extra Ebyte module to the ESP32's pins, exactly like you are doing with the Picos in the field.

Here is why this is the ultimate setup:

  1. It is way cheaper: You save the $39 you would have spent on the shield, replacing it with a $4 part.
  2. It is mathematically guaranteed to work: Because you have an Ebyte module transmitting and an Ebyte module receiving, the radio protocol matches perfectly. The field Pico sends "SWARM", the Hub Ebyte module unwraps it and hands the clean text "SWARM" directly to the LilyGO's ESP32.
  3. The Code is Trivial: Just like the Pico, the LilyGO ESP32 will just use Serial2.readString() to listen for the alert, and then use the cellular modem to text you.

  • Ebyte E220-900T22D (Listening to the Spokes)
  • Solar Panel + 18650 Battery (Keeping it alive 24/7)

  • Action: Hears "TRAP_XX" from the Ebyte, fires up the cellular modem, texts your phone, goes back to monitoring.

turns.response_html:
You have the exact right understanding of the protocols. The LilyGO shield is "raw" (meaning you have to write all the complex radio packet handling yourself), while the Ebyte is cheap and proprietary because it has a tiny factory-programmed chip on it that handles all the complex radio math for you, turning it into a simple wireless serial cable.

To answer your pinch point: Yes, it is incredibly easy to wire and solder the Ebyte module to the LilyGO T-SIM7080G-S3.

In fact, it is exactly as easy as wiring it to the Raspberry Pi Pico. Here is why you have nothing to worry about.

1. The Physical Connections

The LilyGO T-SIM7080G-S3 is a full development board, meaning it has rows of standard 2.54mm (0.1-inch) holes down both sides. These are exactly the same size and spacing as the holes on the Ebyte module.

  • No soldering to test: To build your prototype, you don't even need to use a soldering iron. You can just push standard female-to-female "Dupont" jumper wires onto the pins of the LilyGO and push the other ends onto the Ebyte module.

Because the Ebyte module runs natively on 3.3V, it pairs perfectly with the LilyGO board without frying anything. It is just four wires:

  1. 3.3V Power: Connect Ebyte VCC to the LilyGO 3V3 pin.
  2. Ground: Connect Ebyte GND to any LilyGO GND pin.
  3. Data In: Connect Ebyte RX to a LilyGO Transmit (TX) pin.
  4. Data Out: Connect Ebyte TX to a LilyGO Receive (RX) pin. (You also wire the Ebyte's M0 and M1 pins to ground to lock it in "transmit/receive" mode).

3. The ESP32-S3 "Magic" Routing

Here is the best part about using the LilyGO board (which is powered by the ESP32-S3 chip) for your Hub: You can use almost any pins you want.

Unlike older Arduinos or standard microcontrollers where specific pins are hardwired for TX and RX communication, the ESP32 has a feature called "GPIO Matrix Routing."

This means in your Arduino code, you literally just look at the LilyGO board, pick any two free pins that are easiest for you to solder to, and tell the code to use them.

// Tell the LilyGO that we want to use Pin 4 and Pin 5 to talk to the Ebyte radio
#define EBYTE_RX_PIN 4 
#define EBYTE_TX_PIN 5

void setup() {
  // Start the serial connection on those exact pins
  Serial1.begin(9600, SERIAL_8N1, EBYTE_RX_PIN, EBYTE_TX_PIN);
}

The Antenna Strategy: To Buy or Not to Buy?

That $1 add-on for the Ebyte module is almost certainly a basic SMA "rubber duck" antenna (the short, flexible plastic antennas you see on Wi-Fi routers).

Because you have the Bambu A1, you should design your trap enclosure so the antenna is completely housed inside the plastic box, or shielded by an overhang, to protect it from the elements.

The Hub is the most critical part of your infrastructure. It needs to "hear" whispers from traps located miles away in every direction. Do not use a $1 rubber duck antenna here.

  • Why it matters: Fiberglass antennas are sealed in UV-resistant radomes and are completely waterproof, making them ideal for permanent outdoor installations. More importantly, they provide significantly higher gain (look for a 3dBi to 5.8dBi model). By mounting a fiberglass antenna on a tall pole above the apiary, you dramatically increase the receiving horizon of your Hub, allowing it to easily pick up the weak signals from traps hidden in the trees miles away.

3. The "Extreme Distance" Exception

If you have a specific swarm trap that is pushing that maximum 5 to 6-mile limit, the $1 rubber duck antenna will fail. By pointing the Yagi directly at the apiary hub, you focus all 22dBm of the Ebyte's transmission power into a tight beam, easily punching through 6 miles of Iowa foliage.

That is a sharp, fundamental question about communication theory. In pure digital theory, you are completely right: a 1-bit signal is just the presence or absence of energy (1 = Signal, 0 = No Signal).

So why can’t we just shoot a laser beam, or just listen for a bare "zap" of 915MHz radio energy without caring about packet structures or Ebyte formatting?

It boils down to three massive real-world problems: Environmental Interference, False Alarms in the ISM Band, and Signal-to-Noise Physics.

1. Why Lasers Fail in the Field

A laser is the ultimate 1-bit line-of-sight transmitter, but for a swarm trap, it runs into immediate physical barriers:

  • Line of Sight & Alignment: Aiming a laser beam from a tree branch to an apiary 1 to 2 miles away requires precision optical alignment. If a summer breeze sways the tree branch by just half an inch, your beam will miss the target at the apiary by dozens of feet.
  • Atmospheric Obstacles: Fog, heavy rain, dust, and summer foliage completely scatter laser light.
  • Power: Keeping a laser focused and strong enough to punch through 1 mile of open air requires significantly more power than a tiny radio burst.

2. The 915MHz "Noise Floor" (The False Alarm Problem)

If we drop the laser and use radio, why can't the LilyGO Hub just listen for any 915MHz radio burst and say, "Hey, someone transmitted on 915MHz, that must be Trap 1!"?

The 915MHz frequency is part of the ISM (Industrial, Scientific, and Medical) radio band. It is a completely license-free, open-air "wild west."

At any given moment, the air across rural Iowa is filled with 915MHz radio noise:

  • Utility company smart meters reading power lines.
  • Wireless weather stations in your neighbor's yard.
  • Agricultural soil sensors and pivot irrigation controllers.
  • Garage door openers and car key fobs.

If your Hub only listens for raw radio energy without decoding a payload, your phone will ping you 50 times a day from random background noise, smart meters, or passing trucks.

The proprietary Ebyte packet structure acts like a digital passcode. The Hub ignores the thousands of random 915MHz radio bursts happening around it every hour, and only alerts you when it receives a packet that explicitly decodes to your specific ID code.

3. The LoRa Magic: Operating Below the Noise Floor

This is the most incredible piece of physics regarding LoRa, and the reason raw energy detection doesn't work over long distances.

If you use a simple energy detector (like an old AM radio detector), you can only detect signals that are louder than the background noise. To send a raw pulse 2 miles away, you would need a massive, power-hungry transmitter to "shout" over the background static.

LoRa uses Chirp Spread Spectrum (CSS). Instead of sending a steady pulse of radio energy, it sweeps the frequency up and down in a precise mathematical pattern (a chirp).

Because of this mathematical pattern:

  • A LoRa signal can actually be sent 19 to 20 decibels BELOW the background static noise floor.
  • If you hooked up a raw radio receiver, a LoRa burst 1.5 miles away literally sounds like complete white noise/static. A simple energy detector cannot see it.
  • Only when the receiver decodes the exact mathematical pattern does the signal magically collapse out of the static into a crisp 1-bit alert.

Summary

The Ebyte module's internal formatting isn't just encrypting the text—it is providing the mathematical pattern that allows the receiving module to pull a tiny, weak signal out of a mile of background noise, while simultaneously ensuring that a passing farm truck or smart meter doesn't trigger a false alert.

By having an Ebyte on both sides, you get all that complex digital signal processing for free without having to write a single line of math!

If you do manage to power it correctly (by wiring a heavy-duty external buck converter directly from the 18650 battery to the radio, bypassing the Pico), it will absolutely blast through 10+ miles of trees. If the total price evens out to roughly $20 either way due to shipping, the decision shifts entirely away from cost and over to the engineering differences between the two modules.

Physically, there is zero difference in quality.

  • Ebyte (Chengdu Ebyte) is one of the largest and most respected industrial RF manufacturers in the world.
  • REYAX is a highly reputable Taiwanese engineering firm.
  • Both modules are built using high-end, genuine Semtech LoRa silicon under the metal RF shielding, and both use extremely precise oscillators to prevent frequency drift in cold weather.

However, they take two very different approaches to how they handle the data you give them. Here is how they compare, and why one actually has a slight edge for your specific swarm trap project.

1. The REYAX Advantage: AT Commands & Certification

The REYAX RYLR998 is designed to feel like an intelligent modem.

  • FCC/CE Certified: The REYAX module comes fully FCC certified out of the box. If you ever planned to mass-produce these swarm traps and sell them commercially, having a pre-certified radio module saves you thousands of dollars in legal testing.
  • AT Commands: You talk to the REYAX using explicit text commands. If you want to send the message "SWARM", you don't just send the word. Your Pico has to send AT+SEND=0,5,SWARM (meaning: broadcast to everyone, the message is 5 bytes long, the payload is SWARM).
  • Encryption: The REYAX has AES128 encryption built directly into its firmware, meaning no one can snoop on your bee alerts.

2. The Ebyte Advantage: Transparent Mode & The AUX Pin

The Ebyte E220 is designed to act like a completely invisible wire, and it has one specific hardware feature that makes it the undisputed king of battery-powered devices.

  • Transparent Transmission: Once you configure the Ebyte (by temporarily grounding the M0 and M1 pins), you don't have to wrap your message in complex AT commands. The Pico just prints the text "SWARM", and the Ebyte instantly fires it out of the antenna. It is much simpler to code.
  • The "Killer" Feature (The AUX Pin): The Ebyte module has an extra pin labeled AUX. When you send data into the Ebyte module, the AUX pin physically drops LOW while the radio is transmitting, and snaps HIGH the exact millisecond the radio buffer is empty and the transmission is finished.

Why the Ebyte's AUX Pin Matters for You

Because your swarm trap relies on a tiny 18650 battery and a mechanical limit switch, timing is everything.

If your Pico shouts "SWARM" to the radio and immediately kills its own power, it might kill the power before the radio finishes slowly modulating the LoRa chirp over the air, truncating the message.

You can hit the ground running! You do not need any additional development boards because the Raspberry Pi Pico and the LilyGO T-SIM7080G-S3 are development boards themselves.

Both of these components are designed specifically to be programmed, tested, and debugged right on your desk before you permanently install them in a box out in the woods.

Why You Already Have Everything You Need to Test

  1. Onboard USB Programming:
    • The Raspberry Pi Pico has a built-in Micro-USB port. You plug it into your computer, open a free editor like Thonny, and flash MicroPython scripts directly onto it.
    • The LilyGO T-SIM7080G-S3 has a built-in USB-C port. You plug it into your computer and program the ESP32 chip using Arduino IDE, PlatformIO, or VS Code.
  2. Built-In Voltage Regulation: Both boards take raw power (USB 5V or 18650 3.7V) and step it down to the exact 3.3V required by the chips and Ebyte radios.
  3. Status LEDs: Both boards have controllable onboard LEDs, allowing you to write simple test code to blink an LED when a radio transmission is successfully sent or received.

The "Desk Prototyping" Kit

While you don't need extra boards, there are a few inexpensive workbench accessories you should have on hand to test everything on your desk before heating up the soldering iron:

Recommended Testing Workflow

To make sure your hardware and software are 100% functional before heading out to the apiary, follow this sequence:

  1. Benchtop Serial Test: Plug both the Pico and the LilyGO into your computer via USB. Wire the Ebyte modules using jumper wires on a breadboard. Send a text string from the Pico and verify the LilyGO receives it in the serial monitor console.
  2. Cellular Test: Insert the Hologram SIM into the LilyGO, attach the LTE antenna, and run a test script to trigger an HTTP POST request to a free testing service like Webhook.site.
  3. End-to-End Field Walk: Keep the LilyGO on your desk and walk down the street with the Pico powered by an 18650 battery. Click the limit switch and verify your phone receives the notification over cellular.
  4. Final Assembly: Once the logic is confirmed, solder the wires permanently, snap the boards into your 3D-printed PETG enclosure, and mount them to the trap.
